Content:
When analyzing data, we often want to know how "spread out" the data is. One way to represent the spread of the data is to use the variance of the data.

Content:
If we have a data set that consists of the points [MATH: x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n,] then the variance, denoted by [MATH: \sigma^2,] is defined as

Content:
[MATH: \sigma^2 = \dfrac{1}{n} \sum\limits_{i=1}^n (x_i - \overline{x})^2,]

Content:
where [MATH: \overline{x} = \dfrac{1}{n} \displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^n x_i] is the mean of the data set.

Content:
There's some nice intuition behind the formula for the variance. The mean [MATH: \overline{x}] can be interpreted as the "center" of the data set, and the squared difference [MATH: (x_i - \overline{x} )^2] represents the squared distance between [MATH: x_i] and the center. So, the variance gives the average squared distance of the data points from the center.

Content:
In general,

Content:
- a data set that is spread out over many possible values will have a high variance, while
- a data set that is concentrated (or clumped) near a single value will have a low variance.

Content:
Note: The formula for the variance given here assumes that the points [MATH: x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n] include every member of the population we're interested in. There is a slightly different formula for variance when these points represent a sample drawn from a population. However, we won't worry about the difference for now.

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
When analyzing data, we often want to know how "spread out" the data is. One way to represent the spread of the data is to use the variance of the data.

Content:
If we have a data set that consists of the points [MATH: x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n,] then the variance, denoted by [MATH: \sigma^2,] is defined as

Content:
[MATH: \sigma^2 = \dfrac{1}{n} \sum\limits_{i=1}^n (x_i - \overline{x})^2,]

Content:
where [MATH: \overline{x} = \dfrac{1}{n} \displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^n x_i] is the mean of the data set.

Content:
There's some nice intuition behind the formula for the variance. The mean [MATH: \overline{x}] can be interpreted as the "center" of the data set, and the squared difference [MATH: (x_i - \overline{x} )^2] represents the squared distance between [MATH: x_i] and the center. So, the variance gives the average squared distance of the data points from the center.

Content:
In general,

Content:
- a data set that is spread out over many possible values will have a high variance, while
- a data set that is concentrated (or clumped) near a single value will have a low variance.

Content:
Note: The formula for the variance given here assumes that the points [MATH: x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n] include every member of the population we're interested in. There is a slightly different formula for variance when these points represent a sample drawn from a population. However, we won't worry about the difference for now.

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: A Worked Example

Content:
The variance [MATH: \sigma^2] of a data set is given by

Content:
[MATH: \sigma^2 = \dfrac{1}{n} \sum\limits_{i=1}^n (x_i - \overline{x})^2.]

Content:
[MATH: 1, \: 7, \: 3, \: 9]

First, we need to compute the mean:

Content:
[MATH: x^(―)|= (1)/(n)∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i}; = (1)/(4) ⋅ (1 + 7 + 3 + 9); = (1)/(4) ⋅ 20; = 5]

Content:
Now, we can compute the variance:

Content:
[MATH: σ^{2}|= (1)/(n)∑_(i = 1)^(n)(x_{i} − x^(―))^{2}; = (1)/(4)[(1 − 5)^{2} + (7 − 5)^{2} + (3 − 5)^{2} + (9 − 5)^{2}]; = (1)/(4)[16 + 4 + 4 + 16]; = (1)/(4)[40]; = 10]

Content:
Therefore, the variance is [MATH: \sigma^2 = 10.]

Content:

Content:
[MATH: \sigma^2 = \dfrac{1}{n} \sum\limits_{i=1}^n (x_i - \overline{x})^2]

Content:
It turns out that if we add up all the non-squared differences [MATH: x_i - \overline{x},] then the negatives will cancel out the positives, and the result will always come out to zero no matter how spread out or concentrated the distribution is.

This will happen every time, because the quantity [MATH: \displaystyle \dfrac{1}{n} \sum\limits_{i=1}^n (x_i - \overline{x})] always simplifies to [MATH: 0{:}]
